newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Anglo says looking at future restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Anglo says looking at future restructuring.

text.p: Global mining giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd said on Monday it was reviewing its assets and structure, but stressed that further restructuring was likely to continue in an evolutionary manner.

Anglo director Michael Spicer told Reuters the review of the corporation's assets was ongoing, but that any decisions were hampered by South Africa's rigid foreign exchange controls and other obstacles.
He said that the abolition of exchange controls would play an important part in any restructuring of Anglo but added: "It doesn't mean to say that nothing will happen until then".
"Whilst Anglo does not intend to undergo radical unbundling and believes in diversity, it has made it clear that it adapts to changing circumstances.

"Considerable adaptation has taken place already since the mid-80s. And this process will be ongoing, especially as South Africa fully reintegrates into the world economy," Spicer said in a telephone interview.
The Financial Times reported on Monday that Anglo had launched a strategic review which might lead to the disposal of non-core assets.
But the review was "at an early phase", Spicer said.
The Financial Times report said the review was a response to the upheaval in South Africa following the end of apartheid.
Anglo, the largest mining company in the world, is said to be seeking to expand its international mining interests and earlier this year took a stake in Britain's Lonrho Plc.
Anglo's has vast mining interests in gold, other minerals and the De Beers diamond business in addition to interests in property, consumer industries and heavy industries and financial services.
Spicer said since the early 1990s when South Africa began its transition to democracy after decades of apartheid, Anglo had expanded its international presence.
One of the main areas of expansion was into Africa where Anglo would be spending around 218 million rand in the current financial year on mining exploration alone, the company said earlier this year.
Any plans for expansion by Anglo -- like other South African companies -- are hampered by Pretoria's foreign exchange control regulations.
Spicer said Anglo and other companies were positioning themselves for eventual abolition of exchange control regulations.
"What we have always said, however, is that it is clearly an inhibition. We still are not free to make the sort of decisions that our peer companies are able to make internationally.
"We have to go through very lengthy deliberations with the (central) Reserve Bank as to whether and how.

"All of that makes it immensely more complicated than a RTZ (RTZ-CRA Ltd ) or a BHP (The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd ) which simply identifies an asset, does its studies and says yes or no," Spicer said.
